Destroy
dē-stroi'
v.t. (to ruin, to bring to nothing; rendering Hebrew shachath and shamad, Greek apollumi and kataluo)
From Latin destruere, to unbuild — de, down, and struere, to build. The word is the exact opposite of construction, and Scripture keeps the pairing: the God who destroys is the God who builds, and Jeremiah's commission names both.

Biblical Definition

Destroy is to unbuild, and Scripture applies it to God, to men, and to what men must not do. Abraham's intercession for Sodom opens with the question on which the doctrine of God's justice turns: “And Abraham drew near, and said, Wilt thou also destroy the righteous with the wicked?” (Genesis 18:23). The answer, worked out over six exchanges, is that the Judge of all the earth will do right, and that ten righteous would have spared the city. David refuses a destruction that lay easily within his power and would have ended his exile: “Destroy him not: for who can stretch forth his hand against the LORD'S anointed, and be guiltless?” (1 Samuel 26:9). Rabshakeh claims a divine commission for his campaign — “the LORD said unto me, Go up against this land, and destroy it” (Isaiah 36:10) — a claim that was partly true and wholly presumptuous. And Micah warns that a polluted land will itself destroy those who rest in it (Micah 2:10).

Webster 1828 Definition

To unbuild; to ruin; to bring to nothing. In Scripture it frames Abraham's question whether God will destroy the righteous with the wicked, David's refusal to destroy the LORD's anointed, and the destruction that a polluted land works on those who rest in it.

expand to see more

DESTROY, v.t. [L. destruo; de and struo, to build.] To demolish; to pull down; to unbuild.

2. To ruin; to bring to nought; to annihilate as to usefulness.

3. To kill; to slay; to extirpate.

4. To lay waste; to make desolate, as a country or a city.

5. In Scripture, Wilt thou also destroy the righteous with the wicked? Gen. 18; Destroy him not, 1 Sam. 26.

Key Scripture

Genesis 18:23 — "And Abraham drew near, and said, Wilt thou also destroy the righteous with the wicked?"

1 Samuel 26:9 — "And David said to Abishai, Destroy him not: for who can stretch forth his hand against the LORD'S anointed, and be guiltless?"

Isaiah 36:10 — "And am I now come up without the LORD against this land to destroy it? the LORD said unto me, Go up against this land, and destroy it."

Micah 2:10 — "Arise ye, and depart; for this is not your rest: because it is polluted, it shall destroy you, even with a sore destruction."

Modern Corruption

God's acts of destruction are the standing objection to His goodness. Abraham raised the objection first and in the strongest terms, and Scripture records both his question and the answer, which is that God distinguishes the righteous and does not sweep them away with the guilty.

expand to see more

Genesis 18 is the pattern for every honest wrestling with divine judgment. Abraham does not suppress the question or apologise for it; he presses it six times, from fifty righteous down to ten, and he grounds it in God's own character: Shall not the Judge of all the earth do right? God does not rebuke him. The narrative that follows shows the answer executed — Lot is removed before a single spark falls, and the angel says I cannot do any thing till thou be come thither. Judgment in Scripture is discriminating, and the discrimination is often the part of the story readers skip.

The abuse in the other direction is the claim of a divine mandate for one's own destruction, and Rabshakeh is its portrait. He was not entirely wrong — Assyria was in fact the rod of God's anger — and he was nonetheless destroyed for saying so, because, as Isaiah 10 explains, he meant not so, neither did his heart think so. A man may be an instrument of judgment and be judged for how he wielded it. This is the standing warning to anyone who reads providence as endorsement, and the reason David would not lift his hand against Saul even when circumstance and counsel both urged it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shachath is to mar, spoil, or corrupt as well as to destroy; shamad is to exterminate. Greek apollumi is to destroy or lose, and kataluo is to loosen down, used of the temple and of the law.

expand to see more

Hebrew shachath (H7843) — to mar, spoil, corrupt, destroy; used of the earth corrupted before the flood.

Hebrew shamad (H8045) — to exterminate, to lay waste utterly; the strongest verb of destruction.

Greek apollumi (G622) — to destroy or to lose; the verb behind both perishing and destroying.

Greek kataluo (G2647) — to loosen down, to demolish; I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil.

Latin destruere — to unbuild; de, down, and struere, to build.

Usage

"Of intercession grounded in God's justice: Wilt thou also destroy the righteous with the wicked? (Genesis 18:23)."

"Of restraint toward an enemy in one's power: Destroy him not: for who can stretch forth his hand against the LORD'S anointed (1 Samuel 26:9)."

"Of a polluted land destroying those who rest in it: because it is polluted, it shall destroy you (Micah 2:10)."
